definition.text: A system made of many interacting parts that adapt and learn, whose overall behaviour cannot be predicted from the parts alone.

facts.text: Examples include climate, cities, firms, markets, governments, ecosystems, power grids and ant colonies.
Interactions are non-linear, so small changes in inputs can cause large changes in outputs, and any interaction can feed back on itself.
Such systems often organise themselves rather than following a central hierarchy.
Their high adaptive capacity gives them resilience against disturbance.
They run far from equilibrium and need a constant flow of energy to keep their organisation.
Sociologist Walter F. Buckley coined the term in 1968.
The approach is increasingly used to study economic development and institutional change, where outcomes can be influenced but not precisely controlled.
They are often modelled with agent-based and network models.

definition.text: A view of human systems (economic, social, cultural) and natural systems (water, air, living things, rocks) as linked by two-way interactions.

facts.text: The idea is that human and environmental systems can no longer be studied as separate, isolated systems.
Research frameworks track flows of information, energy, materials, organisms, people and capital between systems, and the agents whose decisions shape them.
Integrated studies reveal feedback loops, non-linearity, thresholds, surprises and legacy effects with time lags that single-discipline work hides.
A foundational study in Wolong Nature Reserve, China, found that subsidies for guarding forests and converting farmland to forest improved panda habitat.
The phrase appears in literature from 1999, and the US National Science Foundation made it a standing research program in 2007.
It builds on social-ecological system theory but covers all aspects of human and natural life, not only social and environmental ones.

definition.text: Interactions between coupled human and natural systems that are far apart, one of four scales in coupled-systems research.

facts.text: Intracoupling studies one coupled system, pericoupling two neighbouring systems, telecoupling two distant ones, and metacoupling all three at once.
A sending system passes a flow to a receiving system, and a spillover system is affected without being the focus.
